'''Dirk Jan Struik''' (September 30, 1894 &ndash; October 21, 2000) was a [[Netherlands|Dutch]]-born [[United States|American]] (since 1934) [[mathematician]], [[historian]] of [[mathematics]], and [[Marxist philosophy|Marxist]] [[theoretician (Marxism)|theoretician]] who spent most of his life in the U.S.<ref name=NYTimes_obit>{{cite journal |last=Saxon |first= Wolfgang |title= Dirk J. Struik; Historian Was 106 |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2000/10/26/us/dirk-j-struik-historian-was-106.html |journal= The New York Times |date=October 26, 2000 |access-date= September 29, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Davis |first1=Chandler |author1-link= Chandler Davis|last2= Tattersall |first2= Jim |last3= Richards |first3= Joan|author3-link= Joan L. Richards |last4= Banchoff|first4= Tom |author4-link= Thomas Banchoff|title=Dirk Jan Struik (1894-2000) |journal= Notices of the American Mathematical Society |volume=48 |issue= 6 |date= June–July 2001 |pages= 584–589 |url= https://www.ams.org/notices/200106/mem-struik.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last= Rowe |first= David E. |author-link= David E. Rowe |title=Dirk Jan Struik, 1894–2000 |journal=Isis |volume=93 |issue= 3 |date = September 2002 |pages= 456–459 |doi=10.1086/374064 |s2cid= 143979122 }}</ref>

==Biography==
=== Early life ===

Dirk Jan Struik was born in 1894 in [[Rotterdam]], Netherlands. His father Hendrik Jan Struik was a grammar school teacher with a passion for mathematics and history. Nearly a century later when Dirk received a Kenneth O. May Medal, he began his acceptance speech with a tribute to Hendrik for cultivating his son's appetite for knowledge.<ref name=Looking_back_article>{{cite journal |author=Rowe, David E. |author-link=David E. Rowe |title=Looking back on a bestseller: Dirk Struik's ''A Concise History of Mathematics'' |journal=Notices of the AMS |year=2001 |volume=48 |issue=6 |pages=590–592 |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200106/rev-rowe.pdf}}</ref> From 1906 to 1911, Dirk attended the [[Hogere Burgerschool|Hogere Burgers School]] in Rotterdam, where he was introduced to [[left-wing politics]] and [[socialism]] by a favorite math teacher, G. W. Ten Dam.<ref>{{cite journal |title=An Interview with Dirk Struik on the Eve of His One Hundredth Birthday |journal=The College Mathematics Journal |volume=33 |url=http://nebula2.deanza.edu/~karl/Sites/Bios/DirkStruikInterview.pdf |via=De Anza College |number=3 |date=May 2002 |pages=178–187 }}</ref>

After entering the [[University of Leiden]] in 1912, Struik showed a strong aptitude for mathematics and [[physics]]. He was taught by the eminent professors [[Willem de Sitter]], [[Hendrik Lorentz]] and [[Paul Ehrenfest]].<ref name=MacTutor_article>{{cite web |title=Dirk Jan Struik - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Struik/ |publisher=[[MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive|MacTutor]] |last1=O'Connor |first1=J. J. |last2=Robertson |first2=E. F. |date=December 1997}}</ref> The unconventional Ehrenfest was said to have exerted the greatest influence on Struik's thinking.<ref>{{cite journal |title=On Connecting Socialism and Mathematics: Dirk Struik, Jan Burgers, and Jan Tinbergen |last=Alberts |first=Gerard |journal=Historia Mathematica |volume=21 |year=1994 |pages=280–305 |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82013307.pdf}}</ref>

In 1917, to help cover university expenses, Struik worked for a while as a high school math teacher. He was next hired as a research assistant to [[Jan Arnoldus Schouten|J. A. Schouten]], a distinguished mathematics professor at the [[Delft University of Technology|Technical University in Delft]]. During this period, Struik developed his doctoral dissertation, "The Application of [[Tensor]] Methods to [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian Manifolds]]."<ref name=MacTutor_article />

In 1922, Struik obtained a doctorate in mathematics from University of Leiden. He was appointed to a teaching position at [[Utrecht University|University of Utrecht]] in 1923. That same year he married [[Saly Ruth Ramler]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Élie Cartan et Saly Ruth Ramler – Médias – MSN Encarta |url=http://fr.ca.encarta.msn.com/media_941562541/%C3%89lie_Cartan_et_Saly_Ruth_Ramler.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240524175255/https://www.webcitation.org/5kwbOiM5G?url=http://fr.ca.encarta.msn.com/media_941562541/%C3%89lie_Cartan_et_Saly_Ruth_Ramler.html |archive-date=24 May 2024 |url-status=dead }}</ref> a Czech mathematician with a doctorate from the [[Charles University of Prague]]. They remained married until her death in 1993.

=== Career ===

In 1924, funded by a Rockefeller fellowship, Struik traveled to [[Rome]] to collaborate with the Italian mathematician [[Tullio Levi-Civita]]. It was in Rome that Struik started pursuing his interest in the [[history of mathematics]]. In 1925, thanks to an extension of his fellowship, he worked with [[Richard Courant]] at the [[University of Göttingen]], where Struik got the opportunity to edit [[Felix Klein]]'s unpublished lectures on 19th century mathematics.<ref name=Looking_back_article/> While there, Struik made extensive use of the university library to research [[Renaissance]] mathematicians.<ref name=MacTutor_article /> He also rekindled interest in a mistaken claim [[Aristotle]] had made that space could be tiled with regular congruent [[tetrahedron|tetrahedra]]. Aristotle's error was first challenged in 1435.<ref>{{cite journal|first=D. J.|last=Struik|author-link=Dirk Jan Struik|title= Het probleem 'De Impletione Loci'|year=1926|journal=[[Nieuw Archief voor Wiskunde]]|series=2nd ser|jfm=52.0002.04|volume=15|pages=121–134}}</ref>

In 1926, Struik was offered positions as a lecturer in mathematics at [[Moscow State University]] and at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT). He decided to accept the latter offer, and spent the rest of his academic career there. He was promoted to assistant professor in 1928, associate professor in 1931, and was made a full professor in 1940.<ref name=Straddled_article>{{cite news |title=Struik straddled worlds of mathematics, Marxist politics |date=14 September 1994 |url=https://news.mit.edu/1994/struik-0914 |newspaper=MIT News |publisher=Institute Office of Communications}}</ref> While at MIT, he collaborated with [[Norbert Wiener]] on [[differential geometry]].<ref name=MIT_obit>{{cite news |title=Mathematician Professor Dirk Struik dies at 106 |newspaper=MIT News |publisher=Institute Office of Communications |date=25 October 2000 |access-date=23 July 2007 |url=https://news.mit.edu/2000/struik-1025}}</ref>

In 1936, Struik co-founded ''[[Science & Society]]''. It would become the world's longest continuously running journal of Marxist scholarship.<ref>{{cite web |publisher=[[JSTOR]] |title=Science & Society |url=https://www.jstor.org/journal/scieandsoci |date=2019}}</ref> He regularly contributed articles to ''Science & Society'', primarily on the [[history of science]].

=== Political controversy ===

Struik was a steadfast believer in [[Marxism]]. Having joined the [[Communist Party of the Netherlands]] in 1919, he remained a Party member his entire life. When asked in 1994, upon the occasion of his 100th birthday, how he managed to still author [[Peer review|peer-reviewed]] journal articles at such an advanced age, Struik replied blithely that he had the "3Ms" a man needs to sustain himself: Marriage (although he was recently a widower at that time), Mathematics, and Marxism.

During the early 1950s [[McCarthyism|McCarthy]] era, Struik's Marxist opinions led to accusations of him being a spy for the [[Soviet Union]]. He was also cited as a "subversive influence in the educational process" in a U.S. Senate committee publication.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=3cIHAAAAMAAJ Subversive Influence in the Educational Process: Hearings Before the Subcommittee to Investigate the Administration of the Internal Security Act and Other Internal Security Laws to the Committee on the Judiciary, United States Senate, Eighty-second Congress, Second Session, Eighty-fourth Congress, First Session]. United States, U.S. Government Printing Office, 1952.</ref> He denied the allegations, and was called before the [[House Un-American Activities Committee]] (HUAC) on July 24, 1951. Struik refused to answer the more than 200 questions asked of him, repeatedly invoking the [[Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fifth Amendment]]'s shield against self-incrimination.<ref name=MacTutor_article /> (He had planned to invoke the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]], but a recent U.S. Supreme Court case struck down that option.) On September 12, 1951, Struik was indicted by a Middlesex County grand jury for "conspiracy to overthrow the governments of the United States and Massachusetts, and for advocating the overthrow by violence of the government of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts". He was released on $10,000 bail.<ref name=Garfinkel_article>{{cite journal |title=How an MIT Marxist weathered the Red Scare |url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2022/06/29/1053203/how-an-mit-marxist-weathered-the-red-scare/ |last=Garfinkel |first=Simson L. |date=29 June 2022 |journal=[[MIT Technology Review]]}}</ref> Soon thereafter, the MIT faculty voted to suspend him, with full salary, until the case was resolved. 

In April 1953, the head of the MIT mathematics department, [[W. T. Martin|William Ted Martin]], testified to the HUAC that he and Struik had both been members of an MIT communist cell between 1938 and 1946.<ref name=Garfinkel_article />

The indictment against Struik was quashed in 1956 by Judge [[Paul G. Kirk Sr.|Paul G. Kirk]] after the [[Massachusetts Supreme Court]] ruled in a different case that the federal [[Smith Act]] superseded state sedition laws. MIT lifted Struik's suspension on May 26, 1956,<ref>{{cite news |title=Struik Suspension Lifted by M. I. T.; Status Unsettled |work=The Boston Globe |date=27 May 1956}}</ref> and he was reinstated as a faculty member.<ref>{{cite news |title= Deaths: Dirk J. Struik, Mathematician |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=October 29, 2000 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2000/10/29/deaths/0218ebef-1294-461b-aa0f-43b6bf69b485/ |access-date=2 October 2018}}</ref> He retired from MIT in 1960.

=== Publications ===

Struik's most celebrated work was ''A Concise History of Mathematics''. Originally published in 1948, it went through four revised editions and was translated into eighteen languages.<ref name=Looking_back_article /> Among his other works that became standard references or textbooks were ''Yankee Science in the Making'' and ''A Source Book in Mathematics, 1200–1800''.

In 1950, Struik published his ''Lectures on Classical Differential Geometry'',<ref>{{cite journal|author=Bompiani, E.|author-link=Enrico Bompiani|title=Review: ''Lectures on classical differential geometry'' by D. J. Struik |journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. |year=1951 |volume=57 |issue=2 |pages=154–155 |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1951-57-02/S0002-9904-1951-09487-2/S0002-9904-1951-09487-2.pdf|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1951-09487-2|doi-access=free}}</ref> which garnered praise from [[Ian R. Porteous]]:
:Of all the textbooks on elementary differential geometry published in the last fifty years the most readable is one of the earliest, namely that by D.J. Struik (1950). He is the only one to mention [[Allvar Gullstrand]].<ref>Porteous, Ian R. (2001) ''Geometric Differentiation'', p. 319, [[Cambridge University Press]]. {{ISBN|0-521-00264-8}}</ref>

In 1971, Struik edited ''The Birth of [[the Communist Manifesto]]''. He began the book with a lengthy essay, "Birth of the ''Communist Manifesto'' and its Historical Significance", that explicates the intellectual and social milieu from which the 1848 ''Manifesto'' emerged. In addition to supplying the full text of the document, with his annotations, Struik included as Appendices all Prefaces by [[Karl Marx]] and [[Friedrich Engels]] for the various language editions of the ''Manifesto'', plus two early ''Manifesto'' drafts by Engels, one of which had just been found at the time Struik's book was published.<ref>{{cite web |title=Birth of the Communist Manifesto |url=https://www.intpubnyc.com/browse/birth-of-the-communist-manifesto/ |publisher=[[International Publishers]] |access-date=27 January 2025}}</ref>

=== Final years, death, and legacy ===

In 1972, Struik was made an honorary research associate in the History of Science Department at [[Harvard University]].<ref name=Straddled_article/> In 1975, he won a Gold Medal of Achievement from the [[National Autonomous University of Mexico|National University of Mexico]] "for his services to the teaching and development of mathematics in Mexico over the years."<ref name=MIT_obit/> In 1989, he and [[Adolph P. Yushkevich]] were the inaugural winners of the [[Kenneth O. May Prize]] in the History of Mathematics.<ref name="Dauben 1999 pp. 1–28">{{cite journal | last=Dauben | first=Joseph W. | title=Historia Mathematica: 25 Years/Context and Content | journal=Historia Mathematica | volume=26 | issue=1 | date=1999 | doi=10.1006/hmat.1999.2227 | pages=1–28| doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="International Mathematical Union (IMU) 2017 r907">{{cite web | title=Kenneth O. May Prize in the History of Mathematics | date=15 November 2017 | website=International Mathematical Union (IMU) | url=https://www.mathunion.org/ichm/prizes/kenneth-o-may-prize-history-mathematics | access-date=1 March 2024}}</ref>

On October 21, 2000, three weeks after celebrating his 106th birthday, Dirk Struik died at his home in [[Belmont, Massachusetts]].<ref name=NYTimes_obit /> A memorial service was held at MIT in the Sala de Puerto Rico room of the student union on campus — a location chosed to symbolize Struik's political sympathies with nations of the [[colonialism|colonial]] and developing world.<ref name=Graham277>Loren R. Graham, ''Moscow Stories.'' Bloomington, IN: Indiana University Press, 2006; p. 277.</ref> The gathering was attended by several hundred people with dozens of frequently politically-charged eulogies delivered by political comrades and personal associates.<ref name=Graham277 />

Struik was memorialized with a short chapter in the book ''Moscow Stories'' by his colleague at MIT, [[Loren R. Graham]], who said that Struik had, when asked, attributed his longevity to "the three Ms — mathematics, marriage, and Marxism."<ref name=Graham276>Graham, ''Moscow Stories,'' p. 276.</ref>

Graham recalled Stuik having been asked by a reporter after the fall of the [[Soviet Union]] whether its collapse and subsequent revelations about the nature of Communism had caused him to reconsider his political beliefs. Struik replied, "No, of course not, because Marxism is an outlook on life. It's the same with Christians; you can be a good Christian despite the fact that Christians have committed horrible crimes in the name of [[Christianity]]."<ref name=Graham276 />

== Books ==
* 1928: Het Probleem 'De impletione loci' (Dutch), Nieuw Archief voor Wiskunde, Series 2, 15 (1925–1928), no. 3, 121–137.
* 1950: ''Lectures on Classical Differential Geometry'', [[Addison-Wesley]].
* 1953: ''Lectures on Analytic and Projective Geometry'', [[Addison-Wesley]].
* 1957: ''[https://archive.org/details/originsofamerica013684mbp/page/n7 The Origins of American Science (New England)]'' via [[Internet Archive]].
* 1971: (editor) ''Birth of the Communist Manifesto'', New World Paperbacks {{ISBN|0-717-80288-4}}.
* 1986: (editor) ''A Source Book in Mathematics, 1200–1800'', [[Princeton University Press]] {{ISBN|0-691-08404-1}}, {{ISBN|0-691-02397-2}} (pbk).
* 1987: ''A Concise History of Mathematics'', fourth revised edition, [[Dover Publications]] {{ISBN|0-486-60255-9}}, {{ISBN|978-0486602554}}.
* 1991: ''Yankee Science in the Making: Science and Engineering in New England from Colonial Times to the Civil War'', second revised edition, [[Dover Publications]] {{ISBN|0-486-26927-2}}, {{ISBN|978-0486269276}}
